questions.question_text: Which is the ascending order of $\frac{1}{3},\frac{1}{8},\frac{1}{5}$?

options.why: This orders denominators rather than fraction values.
This swaps the fifth and eighth despite the denominator rule.
The largest denominator gives the smallest unit fraction.
An eighth is smaller than a fourth.

questions.solution_text:
The smallest denominator is $4$.
$\frac{1}{4}$ is greatest.

questions.question_text: Which fraction lies strictly between $\frac{1}{10}$ and $\frac{1}{5}$?

options.why: A third is greater than a fifth, so it is outside the interval.
This includes the lower endpoint instead of choosing a fraction strictly inside the interval.

questions.question_text: In left-to-right number-line order, which comes first: $\frac{1}{6}$ or $\frac{1}{4}$?

options.why: A fourth is larger and therefore lies farther right.
Different unit fractions do not name the same point.

questions.question_text: Which order is correct for one tenth and one sixth?

options.why: This applies whole-number order without reversing for unit fractions.
Different positive denominators give different unit fractions.

questions.solution_text:
Tenths are smaller parts than sixths.
$\frac{1}{10}<\frac{1}{6}$

questions.question_text: Which list shows $\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{6},\frac{1}{10},\frac{1}{4}$ from greatest to least?

options.why: This is least-to-greatest rather than greatest-to-least.
This places one sixth ahead of the larger one fourth.

questions.solution_text:
Order denominators from smallest to largest: $2,4,6,10$.
$\frac{1}{2}>\frac{1}{4}>\frac{1}{6}>\frac{1}{10}$
